title: Chapter 166 – The Court's Scholar
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Jian]

By the eighteenth day the Annex has become a school, a barracks and a kitchen all at once, and Jian is not sure which of the three he likes best.

Every morning at dawn Duan Ke drills the children in the corridor. He does it with a strict, anxious patience, standing before them in a row, his pale new blade sheathed at his hip and his blistered forearms bound in clean linen. He teaches them to stand. That is all. Ao and Tao stand with their feet apart and their little fists clenched, giggling. Mo Yan stands with her charcoal stub in her teeth. Zhen Li stands as straight as a rod, the brass lamp at his chest. Hai Ren stands in the Great Stillness, which means he does not move at all.

"You are a rock," says Duan Ke, to the two smallest. "Rocks do not wobble. Rocks do not scratch. Rocks do not sneeze."

Ao sneezes.

"A rock that sneezes," says Duan Ke gravely, "is a very bad rock."

Tao collapses with laughter. Jian, watching from the end of the corridor with Bell at his side, has to put his hand over his mouth. Bell does not bother to hide hers. She laughs until she coughs, a deep, helpless, healer's laugh, and wipes her eyes on her sleeve.

"I have not heard that since we left the valley," she says.

"No."

"It is a good sound." She glances at him. "You should do it more."

"I will try."

You won't, says the boy, dryly.

I might.

You'll try. That's different.

* * *

The second incursion comes on the eighth night, and it is smaller than the first.

Three crawlers, none larger than a goat. They come up the same drain, one after another, and Duan Ke meets them at the grate with Hai Ren standing silent at his shoulder. The monk does not fight. He simply stands, and at some point in the engagement the beasts begin to slow, as though the air has thickened around them. They crawl. They stagger. They stop. Duan Ke dispatches each in turn with a single stroke, the pale blade flickering in the amber light, and by the time the last has fallen, the whole affair is over in the space of forty breaths.

"That was your doing," Duan Ke says afterward, wiping the blade.

"It was ours," says Hai Ren.

"I felt it. The slowing."

"It is called the Settling." The monk lowers his hands. "It is not a weapon. It only reminds the body of what it wishes to do. A beast in the dark wishes to hide. I have given it permission."

Duan Ke looks at him for a long moment. Then he says, "Don't ever do that to me."

"I would not."

"Good."

They stand together on the terrace in the lamplight, the swordsman and the monk, while Zhen Li goes along the line behind them lighting the lamps that the beasts have scorched. Jian watches from the stair. He thinks of a hundred and nineteen lamps, and a hundred and ninety-one, and the cracked blue ledger on its lectern. He thinks of Han, on the Wall, and wonders if the old soldier would approve of a child who fights like this.

He would, says the boy.

Would he?

He'd say the boy was too thin. And then he'd give him an extra bowl.

Jian laughs, softly, and has to lean on the rail.

* * *

Ethan is reluctant about the last.

He says so, when Jian goes down on the nineteenth afternoon. He sits in the crystal chamber with his thin hands cupped, and in them the light of the seed has thickened to a warm ember, the size of a plum, and he does not look up.

Mei is at fifty-two percent, he says. She has rested. I tell you that as a courtesy. I would rather not have to tell you the rest.

"Cheng Hui."

Cheng Hui. He nods. The cost is nineteen. She will drop to thirty-three. It is the lowest she has ever been, and I cannot promise that she will climb again before the next incursion.

"Then we wait."

We cannot wait. The old man's mouth tightens. The beasts are coming faster. The panel told you six to nine days between waves. It is now eight. By the time of the third wave, you will need all seven of them standing, and I do not know who among them will be strong enough. He pauses. But that is not why I am reluctant.

"Why, then?"

Because he is the clever one.

Jian waits.

He is nineteen, says Ethan. He is a scholar of the Court. He read the old histories for pleasure. He asks questions that I do not like to answer. When he was awake, in the first days, he asked me one that kept me up for a century. A faint, embarrassed smile. I did not want to wake him. And I did not want to be found out.

"Found out in what?"

Ethan does not answer.

* * *

They wake him at midday.

It is a smaller gathering than before. The children are at lessons. Bell and Nurse stand at the foot of the sixth cot, and Jian sits on the eighth with the rabbit's paw in his hand, and on the stool by the door Yue sits with her palm flat on the floor. The ring of light rises from the rail of the last bed, white and slow. The hum climbs. Mei says, in a murmur, Nineteen, and falls silent.

The young man on the cot opens his eyes.

He does it slowly, almost fastidiously, like a man waking from a nap in a library. His gaze rests on the ceiling for a moment, assessing the plaster. Then he turns his head, with a faint frown, and looks at his hands, which are folded on his chest on top of a thin leather book.

"I appear to have dozed," says Cheng Hui.

His voice is dry and cultured, with the faint, careful vowels of the capital. He is a handsome man, thin-faced and pale, with dark almond eyes and a high forehead, and his black hair is bound in a scholar's knot with a jade pin. His robe is plain gray silk, the collar embroidered with a single thread of red. A red silk marker trails out of the book.

He sits up. He opens the book to the marker and glances at the page, as though checking his place, and then closes it with a small decisive snap.

"I take it," he says, "that this is not the Court."

"No," says Jian.

"Nor the Academy."

"No."

"Nor, I perceive, the afterlife, since there is nothing like enough ceremony." He looks round the Annex with his head tilted, taking in the stove, the lamps, the six sleepers and the faces in the room. "Which leaves a good many options. I shall have to ask the obvious question. Who is in charge?"

"No one," says Bell dryly. "We muddle."

"How admirable." He tucks the book into his sleeve. His eyes come to Jian, and rest there. "You, I think, are the eighth."

Jian starts. "How do you know?"

"The bed. The label. The age." Cheng Hui spreads his hands. "And the way you are holding that rabbit. A man does not hold another child's toy like that unless he has taken responsibility for it." A faint smile. "I am Cheng Hui, Operator Two. A scholar of the Third Hall. I would be grateful if someone would tell me how much of my life I have missed."

* * *

It takes him half a day to read the Hall.

He does it methodically. He begins with Nurse, whom he questions for an hour in the corridor, writing in the margin of his leather book with a pen he produces from nowhere. He proceeds to Bell, and to Duan Ke, and to each of the children in turn, drawing out their stories with a gentleness that Jian had not expected. He asks Ao about the rabbit. He asks Tao about the top. He asks Mo Yan to draw him the Seam, and studies the charcoal for a quarter of an hour, tapping his lip.

By evening he has filled eleven pages.

In the late afternoon he teaches Ao his letters.

It was not planned. The little boy has crept up to the lectern with the rabbit under his arm and stood at the scholar's elbow for ten minutes without a word, watching the pen move. Cheng Hui noticed him on the third minute and went on writing until the end of the line. Then, without looking round, he said, "You may ask."

"What are you doing?" says Ao.

"Recording."

"Why?"

"So that someone, someday, will know what we thought." Cheng Hui dips the pen. "A thing not written is a thing half forgotten. I find that the Court's greatest historians were also its greatest cowards. They knew that what is written can be read, and that what is read can be argued with."

Ao considers this. "Can I do it?"

The scholar lays the pen down. He takes a fresh sheet and a stick of charcoal from the lectern drawer, and sets the boy on the stool beside him, and draws three strokes: a bar, a hook, a dot. "That is the character for rabbit," he says. "In the old script, it looks like a little fellow sitting up."

Ao copies it. The first attempt is a blot. The second is a tangle. The third has a hook that curls like an ear, and Ao lifts it to the light with wide dark eyes.

"It looks like him!"

"It does."

"Do it for Tao!"

"What is Tao?"

"A top," says Ao, with feeling. "It goes round."

Cheng Hui looks at the child for a long moment. Then something in the dry, clever, guarded face shifts, and he draws the character for top. Ao shrieks with delight.

Jian, passing in the corridor, pauses and does not interrupt.

* * *

Nurse keeps a cupboard of Ethan's papers behind the stove.

Cheng Hui finds it on the second day, because he asks where the oldest dust is. He kneels on the Annex floor and opens the doors with a small iron key that Nurse hands him without a word, and inside, on three shelves, lie bundles of thin pale sheets tied in black ribbon. They are covered in a cramped, urgent hand. Notes. Diagrams. Columns of figures that run off the bottom of the page.

He reads for hours. Jian sits with him part of the time, at the other end of the bench, and watches him turn the sheets with the tips of his fingers, delicately, as one handles insects.

"He wrote everything," Cheng Hui murmurs. "Every night. A diary of arithmetic."

"What does it say?"

"A great deal." He holds up a sheet. "This is the third year. He is describing the first seal. He calls it the grace. He says, I do not know whether to call it a mercy or a theft. I have decided to call it a grace, and let the dead decide." A dry little breath. "He did not like himself."

"No."

"And here." Another sheet. "Year eleven. There are four pages torn out. See the stubs? The writing resumes in the middle of a sentence." He turns the page over. "...and so the Ninth, to my relief, did not object."

Jian goes still.

"The Ninth what?" he asks.

"I do not know." Cheng Hui lays the sheet gently on the bench. He is looking at the torn stubs with an expression that Jian has not seen on him before: a kind of sorrowful alertness, like a man who has found a footprint on a path he thought he alone had walked. "But I should very much like to."

* * *

Duan Ke argues with him that night, in the corridor, for twenty minutes.

Jian overhears most of it from the cot. It is not a quarrel; it is something more tentative. The sword boy stands with his arms folded, blocking the way, and the scholar leans against the wall with a book in his hand and a faint smile on his lips.

"You're asking too many questions," Duan Ke says.

"Am I?"

"We have a war. The beasts come every eight days. The old man's dying. The girl's nearly gone. And you want to go through the torn pages of a dead man's diary?"

"He is not dead. He is in a well." Cheng Hui turns a page. "And I would remind you that it was the torn pages that brought the beasts."

"That's not—"

"I do not say it is. I say it may be." The scholar's voice is mild. "A war is won by knowing who the enemy is. You know the beasts, because you have fought them. I wish to know the man who made the Hall in which we are fighting."

Duan Ke scowls. "That's a scholar's answer."

"It is the only one I have." The faint smile widens. "But I notice, my friend, that you have not left."

The sword boy opens his mouth, and shuts it. He stares at Cheng Hui for a long moment. Then, with a gruff sound that might be a laugh, he slumps against the opposite wall and lets his head thump back.

"You're an annoying man," he says.

"I have been told."

"Fine. Read your diary." A pause. "But if you find anything that helps me hit them harder, tell me first."

"I shall put it at the top of my list."

* * *

Jian finds him at the lectern in the corridor, bent over the cracked blue ledger. Cheng Hui has turned it back to the first page, and is reading by the light of one of Zhen Li's new lamps, with his finger moving slowly down the faded brown columns.

"Six hundred and twelve years," he says, without looking up. "Two hundred thousand and four beds. A rate of loss that begins at zero and climbs by a power law until, in the last decade, it is an exponential." He turns a page. "Your Nurse is a careful woman. She never missed a day."

"She loves them."

"That is the only explanation that fits." He closes the ledger and straightens, looking at Jian directly for the first time. "May I be blunt?"

"Please."

"You have woken seven children to fight a war you cannot win."

Jian is silent.

"I do not say it to wound you. I say it because it is the arithmetic. A hall that is failing, a girl who is dwindling, a hundred and ninety dark lamps and a tide of beasts that grows every week." Cheng Hui folds his hands. "You have been saving what you can. That is admirable. But you have not asked the question that matters."

"Which is?"

"Why is the Hall failing?"

"Because the Gate—"

"The Gate fails because it has lost its fuel. Yes. I have heard that." The young man waves a hand. "The names. The returned dead. I follow. But that is a proximate cause. I am asking for the ultimate one." He leans on the lectern, his eyes bright. "A machine that requires the destruction of the dead in order to preserve the living is not a machine. It is a debt. And a debt has a creditor."

* * *

Mei's voice comes through the grille on the morning of the cornerstone, small and cheerful.

I like him, she says. The new one. He asked me what I wanted for breakfast.

Jian smiles in spite of himself. "What did you say?"

That I don't eat. A pause. And he said that was a pity, because he had been looking forward to a decent argument over the tea.

"He is clever."

Very. The light in the grille flickers. I think he's a bit like Papa. He asks things as if the answers might be dangerous. And then he asks them anyway. A sigh. Papa doesn't like it. I can tell. He goes quiet and holds me tighter.

"Does that frighten you?"

A little. Her voice is honest. But I think it's good for him. He has been quiet for six hundred years. It's time somebody made him talk.

* * *

The cornerstone lies at the foot of the great stair, where the dome meets the ground.

Jian reaches it on the arm of Cheng Hui, who has insisted on showing him. They descend the spiral by the light of Zhen Li's lamp, past terrace after terrace of sleeping beds, and at the bottom the walls close in and the air changes. It is cold, and still, and smells of old stone. A single ring of dim blue light shows the way.

The stone stands at the end of a short corridor, in a niche cut into the wall. It is black granite, as he was told, as tall as a man and half as wide, polished smooth. Along its face runs a band of carved characters in a script Jian has never seen: angular, spiky, interlocked. Below the band, a smaller line. Below that, a ring of nine small circles, each one carved into the stone, eight of them smooth and polished and the ninth deeply scratched.

"There," says Cheng Hui.

Jian puts out a hand. The granite is colder than ice. He traces the circles with one finger, the eight smooth ones and the scratched ninth, and a faint prickling runs up his arm.

"What does the band say?"

"What I told Mr. Cole. The Sixth Door. Raised by the Ninth Cohort. For the Rest of All." Cheng Hui lifts the lamp. "And the line below, in a smaller hand: Let none be woken but by the consent of the Nine."

"Nine."

"Nine circles, nine cohorts. Eight smooth, one scored through." The scholar's voice is quiet. "I believe the scoring is more recent. I believe someone defaced it. And I believe that the someone was the man in the well."

Jian traces the scratches. They are deep and ragged, made with something sharp, and they run clean across the face of the ninth circle in a single violent stroke.

He thinks of the cracked blue ledger. He thinks of the torn pages. He thinks of an old man sitting cross-legged in a glass chamber, holding a girl in his hands, and saying for six hundred years that he had built the Hall for her alone.

Brother, says the boy, very quietly. That's a lie.

I know.

He didn't mean it to be.

No. Jian takes his hand from the stone. But it is a lie all the same.

* * *

Yue goes down to the stone herself that night, alone, with a lamp.

Jian does not find out until morning, when Bell mentions it over the broth. The girl had crept out after midnight and walked the cold spiral by herself. She knelt in front of the black granite with her slate in her lap and laid her palm flat against the eighth smooth circle. She stayed there for an hour.

"What did she feel?" he asks.

"She would not say." Bell's mouth is a straight line. "But she wrote something down, and she gave it to me to give you. She wanted you to see it before you went to the shaft."

She hands him the slate. The writing is small and careful, the chalk worn thin.

The stone is not cold like rock. It is cold like a person. When I touched the eight, it was still. When I touched the nine, it was not. It was shaking. I think there is something inside it. I think it is afraid.

Jian reads it twice. He sets the slate on his knee.

"Afraid of what?" he asks.

Bell does not answer. After a moment she takes the bowl from his hands, and sets it on the sill, and says, with a quiet that he has not heard from her before, "I do not think it was the stone she meant."

* * *

They go down to the shaft together, the two of them, at the turn of the evening.

Jian does not know why he agrees. He tells himself it is because Cheng Hui is the first of the seven who has asked what he wants to ask, and he has promised himself, since the table, that he will listen. But as they cross the humming bridge, with the pale light rising round their feet, he is aware of an unease that has no name.

Halfway across the bridge, Cheng Hui stops, and Jian stops with him. The scholar stands with one hand on the cold rail and the other holding his lamp, and he looks down into the pale well of light with an expression of deep and curious pity.

"May I say something before we speak to him?" he asks.

"Of course."

"I do not intend to hurt him." His voice is low. "I have thought about it all afternoon. I believe I know what I am going to ask, and I believe I know that the answer will be painful. But I was raised in a Court where the most terrible thing that could be done to a man was to leave him with his lie. They called it mercy. It was cowardice."

"You think he wants to be asked."

"I think he has been waiting six hundred years for someone to ask. And I think the reason no one has is that all of you love him too much to risk it." The scholar smiles faintly. "Which is, I admit, a fine reason. But it is not an honest one."

Jian says nothing. He looks at the bowed head in the crystal, at the thin shoulders, at the cupped hands.

"Go on," he says at last.

They walk the rest of the bridge together.

Ethan Cole sits in the glass chamber with his head bowed. He does not look up as they approach. He is, Jian thinks, listening to their steps.

Cheng Hui, he says.

"Mr. Cole." The scholar bows, a precise, formal bow, the kind one makes to an elder. "It is an honor. I have wished to speak with you for a very long time."

I know.

"You will remember that I asked you a question once. In the first year. You said you would answer it when I was older."

I remember.

"I am older." Cheng Hui straightens. "By six hundred years, in a manner of speaking."

Ethan's hands tremble on his knees. The seed of light in them flickers, brightens, dims.

You may ask, he says. I will answer if I can.

Cheng Hui takes a breath.

"Mr. Cole. You built the Gate to hold your daughter. You built the Hall to hold the Gate. And you built the eight of us to find a body for her. All of that I understand." He lifts his head. "But Lin Jian and I have been to the foot of the stair. We have read the cornerstone."

I know what it says, whispers Ethan.

"Then you will not mind my repeating it. The Sixth Door. Raised by the Ninth Cohort. For the Rest of All. And beneath, Let none be woken but by the consent of the Nine." The young man's voice is level. "Eight circles polished. One scored through. You told us you built this Hall for one girl, Mr. Cole."

I—

"Then why does the stone say Ninth?"

The seed of light in Ethan's palms flares white, and goes out.

"Who," says Cheng Hui, softly, "were the other eight?"
